title: When the Bell Falls
premise: Ansel Pemberton, a hospice nurse who has spent years hearing the dying count backwards from ten, has built a careful life of rationality around the sound. When the village of Hollowmere's church bell — melted down in 1911 — begins to ring at dusk, the counting spreads beyond the deathbeds: first the old, then the sick, then everyone. Ansel, who has quietly become family to the residents of Marrow House hospice and to Edith Vane, the woman he loves against every rule of his profession, must get them out before the harvest moon completes the bell's final toll. The ending demands the truth Ansel has refused all his life: the bell counts down to a debt owed since 1911, and only a willing voice can answer it — so Ansel stays behind as the others flee, trading his disbelief for their lives, while Edith refuses to let him go alone.
about_author: Casper Delacroix is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent six years in palliative wards across northern England before turning to writing. They live near the coast with two cats and an unshakable habit of listening for bells.

chapters.title: Ten
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At Marrow House, dying Mr. Aldous counts backwards from ten with perfect calm, and Ansel documents it as terminal lucidity, refusing the pattern he's heard for years. He shares tea with Edith, the hospice cook, whose warmth unsettles his professional distance. Emotional beat: quiet dread beneath routine; loyalty to reason established as armor.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. At dusk the village falls silent as a deep bell rings from the roofless tower of St. Maren's — a bell parish records say was melted for scrap in 1911. Only those inside Marrow House seem to hear it clearly. Ansel insists on mass hallucination; Edith crosses herself anyway. Emotional beat: the first crack in Ansel's certainty.

chapters.title: Nine
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The residents begin counting in their sleep, all starting at nine now, synchronized like a congregation. Old Mrs. Tallow wakes weeping, saying she remembers 1911 though she wasn't born yet. Ansel searches the parish archive and finds the bell was recast from a ship's bell that sank with forty souls. Emotional beat: investigation becomes compulsion.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. A tender interlude: the hospice household bands together — games by lamplight, stories, Edith teaching young orderly Sam to bake — while outside the village empties of the living. Ansel realizes these people are his family, not his patients. Emotional beat: love declared softly between Ansel and Edith, duty fraying.

chapters.title: Eight, Seven
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The count accelerates; two numbers fall in one night. Residents who count reach zero briefly — eyes open, bodies still — then resume. A visiting doctor flees mid-sentence. Ansel finds a 1911 ledger: the village sold the bell to fund a lifeboat that never came back. Emotional beat: guilt of a town, weight of history pressing in.

chapters.title: What the Drowned Want
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Mrs. Tallow channels the drowned crew's voices: they were promised the bell would call them home, and it was melted instead. The bell rings itself now, counting toward the harvest moon when the veil thins. Edith begs Ansel to believe; he calculates escape routes instead. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth splits the couple.

chapters.title: Six
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Sam reaches zero and doesn't come back — found standing in the churchyard, smiling wrong. Ansel finally admits aloud that it's real, breaking himself open to Edith. They plan evacuation: one van, seven residents, dawn departure. Emotional beat: confession and resolve; belief arrives too late to be comfort.

chapters.title: The Road Out
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. The exodus — fog thick as wool, the bell audible through engine noise, villagers' empty houses watching. The van fails at the parish line; something walks the hedgerow counting them aloud. Ansel gets the van moving by promising the dark that he'll return. Emotional beat: terror, sacrifice foreshadowed, love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: Five to One
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Safe beyond Hollowmere, Ansel turns back alone as the moon rises; the count plummets — five, four, three — each toll shaking the tower stones loose. In the belfry he finds the 1911 bell's heart, still warm, waiting for a voice to answer its question: will you keep us? Emotional beat: climax; Ansel answers yes, offering his own count instead of theirs.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. As the final toll falls, Edith defies the plan and returns, finding Ansel alive but changed — he hears everything now, every bell, every count. The drowned are released; St. Maren's tower crumbles into silence. Marrow House reopens under new light. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; truth accepted, family kept, love chosen over duty's easy exit.
